questions.q: This lesson uses an unencrypted internal PII data store as an example. Why can leaving it open be architecturally correct at an early-stage startup but unacceptable at a regulated bank?
options: Because unencrypted data is never actually a real risk at any company
Because startups are legally exempt from all data protection obligations
Because banks always have more competent security engineers than startups

Because the right tradeoff depends on each business's regulatory obligations, risk appetite, and stakeholders — the architect's job is matching the response to the actual business, not applying one universal standard
questions.explain: The two architects aren't wrong relative to each other — they're correctly reading two different businesses, with different regulatory exposure, board visibility, and risk appetite.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four business-strategy inputs this lesson says an architect must actually read?
options: The architect's personal preference for a particular vendor's product
Growth strategy — e.g., whether the company is about to acquire another business and inherit its technical debt and attack surface
The office's physical floor plan
The number of open-source libraries used in the codebase
questions.explain: The lesson names risk appetite, growth strategy, competitive position, and cost structure/runway as the real inputs — growth strategy includes acquisitions, new regulated markets, and IPO preparation.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a board funds "this reduces our probability-weighted exposure from $4M to $400K and unblocks deals needing SOC 2" rather than "patch this CVE rated 9.8"?
options: Because CVSS scores are always inaccurate and should never be used
Because boards are legally prohibited from discussing technical vulnerabilities

Because translating technical risk into likelihood and dollar impact is a core architecture deliverable that competes successfully for budget against other business initiatives, unlike a technical severity score alone
Because dollar figures are easier to fabricate than technical scores
questions.explain: An architect who can only speak in technical severity will lose budget conversations to initiatives already translated into revenue or loss-avoidance terms; dollars and likelihood are the business's actual language.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by security being able to act as "a revenue enabler," not just a cost center?
options: Security work, such as achieving SOC 2 or ISO 27001, can directly unlock sales and market access for a B2B company selling to enterprise customers
Security teams should set their own prices for the product being sold
Security budgets should always be larger than product development budgets
Revenue enablement means skipping security reviews to ship features faster
questions.explain: For a B2B SaaS company, a clean SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate is often a genuine sales-enabling asset that unlocks enterprise deals, not merely a defensive cost.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does Enterprise Risk Management (ERM), often structured via the COSO ERM framework, let a mature security architecture function do?
options: Replace the need for any technical risk assessment entirely
Avoid ever reporting security risk to the board
Operate as a fully separate process with no connection to financial or operational risk

Plug the security risk register into the same enterprise-wide risk conversation the board and finance already run, in the business's existing risk language, rather than running a parallel security-only conversation
questions.explain: A mature function connects its risk register to the ERM process boards and finance already use for strategic, financial, operational, and compliance risk, instead of running an isolated conversation that never reaches budget decision-makers.
